young.html: Othello is a great general who serves the city of Venice. He is brave, honest and trusting, and he has married Desdemona, who loves him for the stories of his adventures.

But one of his officers, Iago, secretly hates him. Iago smiles, gives friendly advice, and everyone calls him "honest Iago." Bit by bit, with lies and a stolen handkerchief, he makes Othello believe that Desdemona loves someone else. The play shows how jealousy, once it starts, can grow like a monster.

young.text:
O, beware, my lord, of jealousy;
It is the green-ey'd monster which doth mock
The meat it feeds on.
young.author: William Shakespeare
young.ed: First printed in the First Folio
young.note: Iago pretends to warn against the very thing he is causing. Spelling and punctuation as in the Project Gutenberg text, which modernizes the early printings.

young.html: For parents: Othello ends with Desdemona's murder by her husband and other deaths. Young readers can talk about the play's ideas (trust, lies and jealousy) through a retelling. Charles and Mary Lamb's Tales from Shakespeare (1807) retells the plays as stories for young readers, and is free online.

The rumor game. Whisper a short, true sentence around a circle, each person adding one small change that sounds true. Compare the last version with the first. How did a small lie grow? How could you check a story before believing it?
young.title: Try this: watch a rumor grow

full.html: Shakespeare wrote Othello around 1603–1604, from an Italian tale by Giraldi Cinthio (1565). It is one of his tightest tragedies: after Act I in Venice, the action moves to Cyprus, the enemy fleet is destroyed by a storm, and the danger moves inside, into one man's mind.

Iago gives several reasons for his hatred: Othello promoted Cassio instead of him; he suspects, without evidence, other wrongs. The reasons shift, and the poet Coleridge called his soliloquies "the motive-hunting of a motiveless malignity." Iago tells the audience his plans, so we watch, knowing, as he works on Roderigo, Cassio, Othello and even his own wife.

full.text:
Good name in man and woman, dear my lord,
Is the immediate jewel of their souls.
Who steals my purse steals trash. 'Tis something, nothing;
'Twas mine, 'tis his, and has been slave to thousands.
But he that filches from me my good name
Robs me of that which not enriches him
And makes me poor indeed.
full.author: William Shakespeare
full.ed: First printed in the First Folio
full.note: "Filches" means steals. Spelling and punctuation as in the Project Gutenberg text, which modernizes the early printings.

full.html: The irony is sharp: Iago, praising a good name, is destroying Desdemona's. The word "honest" is used of him again and again.

Othello is a Moor, an African-born general who has served Venice all his life and is honored by its Senate. Desdemona's father objects to the marriage, and Iago and Roderigo use crude insults about Othello's origins. The play shows that prejudice, and many readers think it questions it: Othello is the noblest figure in the play until Iago's lies unmake him. How the play treats race has been discussed by readers and performers for centuries.

The handkerchief, Othello's first gift to Desdemona, becomes the false "proof." Emilia picks it up and gives it to Iago, who plants it with Cassio. In Act V, Othello kills Desdemona; Emilia, learning the truth, reveals her husband's plot; Othello, seeing what he has done, takes his own life. Iago refuses to explain himself.
Thinking Othello is foolish to believe Iago. Everyone in the play trusts Iago. The tragedy is how a good, trusting person can be turned by someone who knows exactly where to press.

items: Why do people believe lies that fit their fears?
Does Iago need a reason to do evil? What does it mean that he will not give one?
How should a play about prejudice be performed today?
What could Othello have done to test what he was told?

deep.html: Iago, who smiles while he plots, is a cousin of the princes Machiavelli describes, who must seem honest while being a fox. Milton's Satan, later on this ladder, is another persuader who works on trust.

questions: Why do you think everyone trusted Iago?
Iago calls jealousy a "green-ey'd monster." Why is jealousy so hard to stop once it starts?
How can you tell whether something you hear about a friend is true?
Iago says a good name is worth more than money. Do you agree?
care: Othello includes a husband's murder of his wife, other deaths, and insulting language about Othello's race used by the villains. This lesson summarizes the plot without detail, quotes none of the insults, and explains how readers have discussed the play's treatment of race.
